The most venomous snake in the world?

Why can’t anyone agree on the most venomous snake?

Or the most dangerous one. Search either question and every list gives a different answer. Most of them aren’t wrong. They are answering different questions, often with numbers nobody can trace.

Why the lists disagree

They measure different things

“Most toxic venom”, “most venom per bite” and “kills the most people” are three separate questions, and each has a different answer.

Most toxic (mice): inland taipan · Largest yield in our data: forest cobra · Biggest killers: vipers in South Asia and Africa

Lab tests aren’t done the same way

Venom injected into a vein, the belly or under the skin gives a different number for the same snake. Lists often mix them.

4 injection routes in use: SC, IV, IP, IM

Numbers get copied without sources

Figures pass from list to list until nobody knows where they came from. Some turn out to be wrong.

Hook-nosed sea snake: 0.02 (untraced) vs 0.164 mg/kg (published study)

Danger depends on people too

A snake with deadly venom that lives in a remote desert kills fewer people than a common snake near farms and villages with no antivenom nearby.

Inland taipan: no deaths in Australia 2005–2015 (Australian Snakebite Project)

How we tackle it

Separate the questions

Two scores, not one ranking

Venom Hazard asks how dangerous the venom itself is. Human Risk asks how likely a bite is to happen and go badly.

Show the evidence

Every number has a source

Each figure is graded A to D by how well it traces back to an original study.

Keep the disagreements

Conflicts are flagged, not hidden

When sources differ by more than 1.5 times, the species is flagged and every figure stays on record.

Open method

You can check our working

How each score is built, step by step, from LD50 and venom yield to the four risk factors. Scores explained.
